newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ Labour holds olive branch to Alliance.
newsitem.headline: NZ Labour holds olive branch to Alliance.

text.p: New Zealand Labour leader Helen Clark held out an olive branch to the left-wing Alliance on Thursday, saying she hoped the two parties could talk business after next month's election.
Clark sounded a conciliatory note towards Alliance leader Jim Anderton in a televised debate between party leaders.
"I know that Labour can lead the next government. I am prepared to reach out to other political parties which share a number of common objectives," Clark said.

"Jim Anderton and I have agreed on a lot in the past. There are things in economic policy we don't agree with...We know where the differences are. After the election, Jim, I would like to be talking to you and your people..."
Labour and the Alliance share common ground in wanting to repeal the union-busting Employment Contracts Act and in some areas of health, education and housing policy.

The Alliance, however, is more interventionist and protectionist, campaigning to reverse the sale of state-owned Forestry Corp to a Fletcher Forest-led consortium including China's Citic. It wants to reshape the Reserve Bank Act to make the central bank target growth and employment as well as price stability.

Labour and the Alliance, along with economic nationalist New Zealand First, are drawing around 50 percent support in opinion polls. If they can work together, they could oust the conservative National Party government.
National has about 38 percent and its re-election chances depend mainly on the free-market ACT and morals-based Christian Coalition, neither of which is certain of winning seats.
The left remains split, however, by Labour's refusal to countenance pre-election coalition deals despite repeated overtures from the Alliance.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger said the election, New Zealand's first under proportional representation, was a choice between stable leadership and a three-headed coalition of parties "united only in their gloom".

New Zealand First's Winston Peters stressed opposition to asset sales, telling viewers: "We want a society back in control of its destiny, where New Zealand is run by New Zealanders, for New Zealanders."

Anderton appeared to score points with the studio audience when he spoke of the creation of a two-tier health system, arguing only those who could afford private health insurance were guaranteed first-rate care.

Television One said a group of 80 people awarded clear victory in the debate to Labour's Clark. Forty-one percent rated her the winner, against 31 percent for Peters, 15 percent for Anderton and 13 percent for Bolger.
